SPACE CLEANER — Project Summary
SPACE CLEANER is a 3D educational game designed to raise awareness of the dangers of space debris and demonstrate how it can be detected, monitored, and safely removed. Players assemble and launch their own rockets, explore Earth's orbit, identify space debris using radar systems, assess collision risks, and use robotic arms to capture and remove hazardous objects.

Inspired by real-world research and technologies developed by NASA, ESA, the Canadian Space Agency, and Astroscale, the game combines realistic 3D visuals, interactive missions, sound effects, and educational information. It also supports Mongolian and English languages.

The main goal of SPACE CLEANER is to help players understand the growing problem of space debris, learn about collision prevention and removal technologies, and develop awareness of the importance of protecting Earth's orbital environment for future generations.

Project Documentation & Research Specification

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project Report, Research, and Development Plan

The primary goal of this report is to develop SPACE CLEANER not merely as an arcade game that shoots and destroys space trash, but as a 3D educational simulation that teaches players the real dangers of orbital debris, how it is detected, how collision risks are assessed, and how safe removal operations are conducted.

Verification Note: The current game code, buttons, and function behaviors were not directly inspected or verified via the AI Studio link in this session. Therefore, this report consolidates all requirements, recommendations, and revision histories from prior discussions. Any feature whose implementation has not been verified is treated as unimplemented.

1. Core Problem Statement: Why It Matters, Existing Technologies, and Our Unique Advantage

Before detailing system architecture and development milestones, this opening section addresses three foundational questions defining the purpose and value of SPACE CLEANER.

1.1 Why Should We Pay Attention to Space Debris?

Modern daily life relies heavily on satellites in Earth orbit for weather forecasting, global navigation (GPS), telecommunications, and Earth observation. However, decades of spaceflight have left behind non-functional satellites, spent rocket stages, and millions of collision fragments traveling at orbital speeds.

  • Extreme Kinetic Energy: Because objects in Low Earth Orbit (LEO) travel at roughly 7–8 km/s, even a fragment larger than 1 cm carries enough kinetic energy to severely damage or disable an operational spacecraft.
  • Cascading Risk (Kessler Syndrome): Every collision generates thousands of new fragments, increasing the probability of further collisions in crowded orbital bands and threatening long-term access to space.
  • Public Misconception: Popular media often portrays space cleanup as blasting debris apart with lasers or explosives—an action that in reality multiplies fragments and worsens orbital hazards.

1.2 Does This Technology Already Exist?

Yes—real-world space agencies and aerospace companies are actively developing and testing key elements of orbital monitoring, rendezvous, and active debris removal, though large-scale routine cleanup remains an emerging frontier:

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 1 of 15

  • Orbital Tracking & Conjunction Assessment: Systems such as NASA’s Orbital Debris Program, Canada’s NEOSSat and Sapphire surveillance satellites, and the CRAMS risk-assessment service continuously track objects and calculate collision probabilities.
  • Rendezvous & Proximity Inspection: In 2024–2026, Astroscale’s ADRAS-J mission (under JAXA’s CRD2 program) demonstrated safe approach, inspection, and characterization of a derelict upper-stage rocket body in orbit.
  • Robotic Capture & Deorbiting: The European Space Agency’s ClearSpace-1 mission (planned for launch in 2029) is designed to capture a derelict satellite (PROBA-1) using a four-armed robotic capture mechanism and guide it into a controlled atmospheric reentry.

1.3 What Makes SPACE CLEANER Unique?

While conventional space games focus on high-speed combat and destruction, SPACE CLEANER introduces a distinctive educational and simulation-driven approach:

  • Scientific Realism Over Destruction: Players are explicitly penalized for fragmenting debris; success requires careful proximity maneuvering, robotic capture, stabilization, and controlled deorbiting or graveyard-orbit relocation.
  • End-to-End Engineering Workflow: Rather than skipping straight to action, players experience the complete real-world operational chain: Rocket Assembly → Launch → Radar Detection → Collision Risk Assessment → Robotic Capture → Safe Removal → Post-Mission Analysis.
  • Grounded in Verified Space Programs: Every mission briefing, risk warning, and post-task insight connects gameplay mechanics directly to real missions and data from NASA, ESA, CSA, and Astroscale, offered cleanly in both Mongolian and English.

2. Project Overview & Background

Project Name: SPACE CLEANER
Core Focus: A 3D educational game demonstrating space debris detection, collision risk awareness, and safe removal using robotic systems.
Target Platforms: Android and iOS (iPhone).
Visual & Graphic Direction: Realistic 3D environment, accurate representation of orbital space, intuitive user interface, and smooth animated workflows.

Humanity operates a wide variety of spacecraft in Earth orbit, including communications satellites, space stations, and launch vehicles. Decommissioned satellites, spent rocket stages, and collision fragments remain in orbit and pose persistent hazards to active spacecraft. Because even tiny fragments move at hypervelocity speeds, SPACE CLEANER is designed to teach players:

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 2 of 15

  • How space debris is generated in Earth orbit.
  • Why collisions between orbital objects are uniquely dangerous.
  • How fragments created by a collision compound risk for neighboring satellites.
  • How debris is detected, tracked, and approached safely.
  • How robotic arms and capture mechanisms safely remove hazardous objects.
  • Why preserving the long-term sustainability of the orbital environment is essential.

3. Core Gameplay Objectives & Operational Sequence

The gameplay loop is structured to follow a logical seven-stage operational sequence:

  1. Stage 1 — Rocket Assembly: The player selects core rocket components and equips engines, fuel tanks, guidance systems, and robotic capture hardware. Selected configurations directly govern mission capabilities.
  2. Stage 2 — Rocket Launch: The assembled rocket launches into orbit. Launch visuals, flight dynamics, and audio effects must match the exact rocket configuration built by the player.
  3. Stage 3 — Space Debris Detection: Radar and telemetry displays present debris locations, trajectories, and approximate distances. The player selects a target object.
  4. Stage 4 — Collision Risk Assessment: The system visualizes whether debris trajectories intersect. When a high-probability conjunction appears, an alert prompts the player to prioritize which object to remove or mitigate first.
  5. Stage 5 — Robotic Arm Capture: The servicing spacecraft slowly approaches the target and extends its robotic arm. Approach, capture, and stabilization are presented as distinct, clearly readable steps.
  6. Stage 6 — Safe Removal: The captured object is transferred to a safe disposal orbit or guided into a controlled atmospheric reentry according to mission parameters. Blasting or shattering debris into smaller fragments is never rewarded as cleanup.
  7. Stage 7 — Mission Debrief: Displays objects removed, objectives completed, resources consumed, risk reduced, and score earned. If an error occurs, the cause is explained and the player can retry.

4. Mandatory Educational Content

The defining strength of SPACE CLEANER is ensuring players understand why each engineering step is necessary rather than simply pressing buttons.

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 3 of 15

4.1 Categories of Space Debris

Debris Category

In-Game Representation

Decommissioned Satellite

Large, inactive spacecraft remaining in orbit

Rocket Stage

Upper-stage booster left in orbit after payload deployment

Collision Fragment

Debris pieces generated by an impact between two objects

Small Fragment

Low-visibility, high-velocity hazard posing severe impact risk

Operational Spacecraft

Active satellites and stations requiring protection

4.2 Understanding Collision Hazards

To teach conjunction dynamics accurately, the game must demonstrate the following sequence:

  1. Two orbital objects travel along intersecting or converging trajectories.
  2. Their orbital paths draw close, creating a measurable collision risk.
  3. An on-screen risk alert notifies the player of the conjunction.
  4. If a collision occurs under mission conditions, numerous small fragments are generated.
  5. The simulation explains how those new fragments threaten other active satellites.
  6. The player executes preventive tracking and removal missions to mitigate the hazard.

Scientific Accuracy Note: Not every close approach results in a collision. When displaying approaching objects, the interface should distinguish between collision probability, closest approach distance, and positional uncertainty.

4.3 The Kessler Syndrome

The Kessler Syndrome describes a cascading scenario in which collisions between orbital objects generate new debris fragments, which in turn increase the likelihood of further collisions:

  • An initial collision produces a cloud of fragments.
  • Those fragments disperse across orbital altitudes and inclinations.
  • Some fragments pass near other spacecraft, creating secondary collision hazards.
  • Demand for active monitoring, collision avoidance, and debris mitigation rises sharply.

This phenomenon does not mean all orbits collapse instantaneously; the game should present it accurately as a long-term escalating risk scenario.

5. Consolidated Development Requirements & Fixes

The following specifications consolidate all design, visual, and functional requirements established in prior reviews.

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 4 of 15

5.1 Earth Visualization

  • Render Earth realistically in natural blues and greens.
  • Include dynamic cloud layers and an atmospheric limb glow.
  • Fix camera framing issues that make Earth appear overly distant or disproportionately tiny.
  • Scale background celestial and orbital elements appropriately for screen readability.
  • Adjust camera angles dynamically to match each gameplay phase.
  • Maintain clear visual scale proportions among the rocket, Earth, and debris objects.

5.2 Rocket Assembly & Launch

  • Ensure the player’s custom-assembled rocket does not revert to a generic model during launch.
  • Use the exact same rocket model across the assembly bay and launch sequence.
  • Deliver smooth, physically believable launch acceleration and trajectory motion.
  • Synchronize appropriate launch audio effects with ignition and ascent.
  • Transition seamlessly from upper-atmosphere ascent into the orbital environment.

5.3 Robotic Arm & Capture Operations

  • Prevent the robotic arm from snapping or teleporting abruptly onto a target.
  • Execute a gradual, controlled approach toward the target object.
  • Animate arm extension in distinct, mechanical stages.
  • Ensure accurate physical contact and latching between the end-effector and the target.
  • Show the captured debris moving rigidly together with the robotic arm once secured.
  • Position the camera so the player can clearly observe the capture alignment.
  • Visually differentiate between successful capture and failed/missed capture attempts.
  • Depict controlled deorbiting or disposal maneuvers clearly and realistically.

5.4 Screen Transitions

  • Eliminate abrupt cuts between game screens.
  • Prevent sudden jumps in object position or scale during screen transitions.
  • Display clear progress indicators during loading states.
  • Maintain logical continuity from one mission stage to the next.
  • Never advance to the next screen before the current action finishes completing.

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 5 of 15

5.5 User Interface (UI)

  • Ensure warning banners and explanatory text never clip or overflow off-screen.
  • Prevent mid-word line breaks or truncated sentences.
  • Divide lengthy explanations into 3–4 concise, digestible paragraphs or bullet points.
  • Use clear, concise phrasing across all prompts.
  • Display Mongolian and English versions cleanly and separately without overlap.
  • Adapt UI layouts responsively across varying mobile screen aspect ratios.
  • Verify that every primary button executes its intended action reliably.
  • Update on-screen telemetry immediately after every player action.

5.6 Error Recovery & State Rollback Rules

To protect gameplay integrity, the system must enforce six defensive state rules:

  1. Save a verified valid game state immediately before initiating a critical action.
  2. If an action fails, display a clear explanation of the error cause.
  3. If game state corruption occurs, automatically roll back to the last verified valid state.
  4. Provide an accessible Retry button.
  5. Never erase previously completed mission progress due to a localized failure.
  6. Debounce button inputs so double-taps cannot trigger duplicate actions.

5.7 Audio Design Specifications

Game Event

Recommended Audio Cue

Rocket Assembly

Soft mechanical click

Rocket Launch

Low-frequency thruster rumble

Reaching Orbit

Gradually tapering engine cutoff sound

Radar Sweep

Short electronic pulse/ping

Hazard Detected

Subtle, non-jarring warning chime

Robotic Arm Movement

Controlled servo/mechanical actuator hum

Brief celebratory harmonic cue

Action Error

Moderate, non-harsh alert tone

Audio Requirement: Sound effects must reinforce situational awareness without causing listener fatigue or distraction. Include dedicated mute and volume controls.

Localization & Official Emblem Rules: English sentences must never mix into the Mongolian interface, and Mongolian words must never appear in the English interface. Official agency names (such as NASA, ESA, Canadian Space Agency, and JAXA) remain in their standard official forms. Any depiction of the State Flag of Mongolia must strictly adhere to official colors, aspect ratios, and Soyombo emblem proportions.

6. Comparative Research on Real-World Space Programs

This section grounds SPACE CLEANER’s mechanics in verified scientific and aerospace initiatives.

6.1 NASA — Orbital Debris Research & Mitigation

The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) leads extensive research into tracking, modeling, and preventing orbital debris (Source: NASA Orbital Debris FAQ). Key takeaways for the game include:

  • Even millimeter- and centimeter-scale fragments can inflict critical damage on spacecraft.
  • Preventing the creation of new debris is the single most effective mitigation measure.
  • Active debris removal poses major technical and economic challenges.
  • Educating operators and the public on collision risks is vital for space sustainability.

In-Game Application: Beyond capturing existing debris, players complete missions focused on debris prevention, such as passivating end-of-life satellites and executing controlled disposal maneuvers.

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 7 of 15

6.2 ESA — ClearSpace-1

The European Space Agency’s (ESA) ClearSpace-1 mission is designed to demonstrate the capture and safe deorbiting of an uncooperative, derelict object using robotic arms:

  • Target Object: ESA’s PROBA-1 satellite (approximately 95 kg).
  • Capture Mechanism: Four-armed robotic capture system.
  • Planned Schedule: Published ESA plans list a target launch in 2029 (a planned date, not an already completed launch).

In-Game Application: Model realistic robotic arm kinematics; observe target spin and attitude before approach; evaluate orientation prior to capture; stabilize the target after grasping; and execute disposal as a separate phase.

6.3 Canada — Space Situational Awareness & Risk Assessment

The Canadian Space Agency (CSA) supports orbital sustainability through space surveillance and conjunction risk analysis:

  1. NEOSSat: A microsatellite used to track orbital objects and collect space situational awareness data.
  2. Sapphire: An electro-optical surveillance satellite contributing to Canada’s space object tracking capabilities.
  3. CRAMS (Conjunction Risk Assessment and Mitigation System): A service that evaluates close approaches and collision probabilities to support avoidance maneuver planning.

In-Game Application: Require players to review radar telemetry, proximity calculations, and risk assessments before initiating capture. Players inspect object ID, type, velocity vector, distance, conjunction warnings, and recommended actions. Note: Because these Canadian systems perform tracking and risk assessment rather than physical capture, they must not be described as debris-grabbing robots.

6.4 Astroscale — ADRAS-J

Astroscale’s ADRAS-J mission demonstrated safe rendezvous and proximity inspection of a large derelict object:

  • Launched on February 18, 2024, as part of Phase I of JAXA’s Commercial Removal of Debris Demonstration (CRD2) program.
  • Successfully approached and inspected an upper-stage rocket body, concluding mission operations and initiating its deorbit phase on March 25, 2026, as reported by Astroscale.

In-Game Application: Require the servicing craft to hold at a safe standoff distance first to inspect the target’s shape, orientation, and tumble rate, allowing players to orbit the camera around the target before final approach. Clarify in game notes that ADRAS-J was a proximity inspection demonstration rather than a physical removal mission.

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 8 of 15

6.5 NGOs & International Cooperation

The ESA Zero Debris Charter is a global initiative promoting long-term orbital sustainability across space agencies, private companies, universities, and non-profit organizations. Signatories include non-governmental organizations such as Cosmos for Humanity, alongside over 250 organizations across 35 countries as of September 2026.

Institutional Distinction: An NGO is a non-governmental organization, ESA is an intergovernmental space organization, and the Canadian Space Agency is a national government agency. Signatories to the Zero Debris Charter should not be labeled as active debris-removal operators unless verified.

In-Game Application: Incorporate international cooperation missions where players receive telemetry from partner organizations and coordinate joint sustainability tasks.

6.6 ESA Space Environment Reports (2025 & 2026)

ESA’s 2025 Space Environment Report (covering data through the end of 2024) noted roughly 40,000 tracked objects in Earth orbit and estimated over 1.2 million debris fragments larger than 1 cm. Additionally, ESA’s September 2026 update reported over 300 launches and more than 4,000 new payloads placed into orbit during 2025. Every statistic displayed in the game’s educational database should include its source and publication date.

8. Proposed Feature Enhancements

Beyond baseline fixes, the following enhancements will deepen educational value and replayability.

8.1 Progressive Mission Tier System

  • Tier I — Basic Debris Detection (Beginner): Locate and catalog a small number of orbital objects using radar.
  • Tier II — Conjunction Risk Analysis (Intermediate): Track two or more converging objects and evaluate collision risk levels.
  • Tier III — Robotic Capture Operations (Advanced): Execute a controlled rendezvous and capture a large derelict object.
  • Tier IV — Multi-Object Threat Prioritization (Expert): Analyze a crowded orbital sector, prioritize the highest-risk target, and execute a multi-step removal plan.

8.2 Enhanced Radar Telemetry System

Radar should function as an active analytical instrument rather than cosmetic decoration, displaying Object ID, Object Type, Velocity Vector, Approximate Distance, Risk Level, Tracking Status, and Conjunction Alerts:

  • Low Risk: Routine monitoring required.
  • Medium Risk: Re-verify conjunction trajectory and closest-approach data.
  • High Risk: Immediate assessment and mitigation action required.

Note: These three tiers serve as clear educational gameplay classifications rather than official operational thresholds used by space agencies.

8.3 Modular Servicing Equipment

Players can customize their servicing spacecraft with optical camera suites, laser rangefinders, articulated robotic arms, capture mechanisms, communications arrays, and attitude control thrusters. Each module carries distinct operational trade-offs that influence mission strategy.

8.4 Micro-Learning Scientific Takeaways

Each mission stage displays a concise 1–2 sentence scientific takeaway:

  • After a Collision Event: “When two orbital objects collide, they can generate hundreds of high-speed fragments that threaten nearby operational satellites.”
  • Before Robotic Capture: “Observing a target’s orientation and rotation rate from a safe standoff distance is essential before attempting capture.”
  • Upon Mission Completion: “Safely removing defunct spacecraft from crowded orbits helps preserve a sustainable space environment for future missions.”

9. Technical Architecture & Development Recommendations

Previous discussions referenced a project link hosted in the Google AI Studio Build environment. Rather than assuming a full engine rewrite, development should preserve the existing working codebase, libraries, and component structure while isolating subsystems cleanly.

9.1 Protecting the Existing Build

  1. Preserve all currently functioning features and modules.
  2. Avoid rewriting the entire project from scratch.
  3. Introduce one major architectural change at a time.
  4. Verify core functionality immediately after every modification.
  5. Revert to the last known working build if a regression occurs.
  6. Ensure UI layout adjustments never break core simulation logic.

9.2 Modular Subsystem Separation

  • Rocket System: Rocket assembly, component configuration, and launch physics.
  • Earth Environment: Earth globe, cloud layers, atmosphere, and orbital lighting.
  • Debris System: Debris categories, orbital trajectories, and spatial coordinates.
  • Radar System: Object scanning, telemetry readout, and target selection.
  • Risk Assessment: Conjunction calculation and collision probability alerts.
  • Robotic Arm System: Articulated arm kinematics, approach, and grappling.
  • Removal System: Controlled deorbit and disposal orbit transfer sequences.
  • Mission System: Tier progression, scoring rubric, and objectives.
  • UI System: Menus, HUD overlays, alerts, and educational panels.
  • Audio System: Event-driven sound effects and volume controls.
  • Localization: Complete, isolated Mongolian and English language tables.

SPACE CLEANER — Integrated Project ReportPage 11 of 15

9.3 Mobile Readiness (Android & iOS)

To ensure smooth performance on Android and iPhone devices, the build must support responsive UI scaling across screen aspect ratios, touch-friendly button sizing, responsive camera gesture controls, optimized 3D rendering workloads, accessible audio volume controls, offline playability for core educational modules, and selectable graphics quality presets matched to device hardware.

10. Implementation Roadmap & Verification Checklist

  1. Phase 1 — Bug Fixes & Stabilization: Repair non-responsive buttons, broken screen transitions, UI clipping, and language toggles.
  2. Phase 2 — Visual & Kinematic Polish: Upgrade Earth rendering, rocket model consistency, debris scale, camera framing, and robotic arm animations.
  3. Phase 3 — Radar & Risk Engine: Implement object telemetry, trajectory vectors, conjunction warnings, and risk tiers.
  4. Phase 4 — Capture & Safe Removal Loop: Integrate standoff inspection, robotic grasping, stabilization, and controlled disposal.
  5. Phase 5 — Educational Layer & Scoring: Add micro-learning explanations, post-mission quizzes, and the multi-criteria scoring system.
  6. Phase 6 — Audio & Smooth Transitions: Integrate calibrated sound effects, animations, and seamless screen transitions.
  7. Phase 7 — Mobile Device Testing: Validate layout, frame rate, touch controls, and responsiveness on Android and iOS hardware.

11. 30-Second Pitch & Demo Script

To present the concept concisely in a 30-second video showcase, the sequence is divided into two 15-second segments:

  • Part 1 (0–15 Seconds — The Space Debris Threat): Open on Earth from orbit; reveal operational satellites and derelict rocket stages; highlight two converging trajectories; trigger a collision risk warning; briefly illustrate the hazard of fragment generation.
  • Part 2 (15–30 Seconds — The Solution: SPACE CLEANER): Launch the servicing rocket; approach a derelict target; extend the robotic arm and secure the object; execute a safe deorbit maneuver; display the SPACE CLEANER title and mission statement.

Core Tagline: “Space debris threatens future space exploration and the satellites we rely on every day. SPACE CLEANER — learn how we protect Earth’s orbital environment through interactive simulation.”

14. Final Conclusion

SPACE CLEANER offers strong educational potential by transforming space debris mitigation into an interactive, scientifically grounded experience. Its primary advantage lies in rejecting arcade-style destruction in favor of teaching the authentic engineering chain: debris formation, orbital mechanics, conjunction risk assessment, robotic proximity operations, and safe disposal.

Drawing directly on verified programs from NASA, ESA (ClearSpace-1), CSA (NEOSSat, Sapphire, CRAMS), and Astroscale (ADRAS-J), the development team should adhere to seven core principles:

  1. Maintain strict scientific accuracy across all telemetry, visuals, and explanations.
  2. Clearly illustrate the cascading hazards of orbital debris and collisions.
  3. Model radar, rocket, and robotic arm operations on real aerospace engineering.
  4. Enforce safe capture and controlled disposal rather than explosive fragmentation.
  5. Deliver complete, error-free Mongolian and English localizations.
  6. Ensure rock-solid button responsiveness, screen transitions, and state recovery.
  7. Leave every player with clear, memorable scientific knowledge after each mission.
